icicle.e: From Middle English isykle, isikel, from Old English *īsġicel, from Proto-West Germanic *īsajikil, *īsajekul, equivalent to ice + ickle. It was assimilated to nouns in -icle, from Latin -iculus—the expected spelling would have -ickle. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Iesjuukel (“icicle”), German Low German Iesjökel, dialectal Danish jisegel (“icicle”), Norwegian isjukel (“icicle”) and Elfdalian aisikkel.

s.d: ice resembling a pendent spear, formed by the freezing of dripping water
A drooping, tapering shape of ice.
x: Several days of sub-zero temperatures caused icicles up to 1.5 metres long to form in tunnels across Greater Manchester, Lancashire and Cumbria.

s.d: Old World annual widely naturalized in warm regions having white flowers and fleshy foliage covered with hairs that resemble ice
A plant in the daisy family, Asteraceae, with long, powdery-white leaves (Helichrysum thianschanicum).

x: The cold Alpine air flowed icily into his car, so he stopped by the roadside to put on a leather trench-coat, thick scarf, and woollen hat[…]

Bond had pulled her head back by her hair and had kissed her once, long and cruelly. Then he had told her to go to sleep and had leant back and waited icily for his body to leave him alone.

a plastic or metal utensil used for cake and pastry decoration, similar in principle to a pastry bag.

icky.e: 1935, American English; from icky-boo (circa 1920): sickly, nauseated; baby talk corruption of sick; from a sentimental term for jazz music.

s.d: very bad
x: a lousy play
it's a stinking world

s.d: soft and sticky
(informal) Unpleasantly sticky; yucky; disgusting.
x: I stepped in something icky and it smells terrible.
Crew member Sachin Sharma of India said workers had no problems with being thrust into the icky job of handling the red bags filled with human waste.

s.d: (informal) Excessively sentimental.
(informal) Unwell or upset; in a bad state of mind or health.
x: I'm not going to work today. I just feel icky.

icon.e: From Latin īcōn, from Ancient Greek εἰκών (eikṓn, “likeness, image, portrait”). Eastern Orthodox Church sense is attested from 1833. Computing sense first recorded in 1982.

s.d: (computer science) a graphic symbol (usually a simple picture) that denotes a program or a command or a data file or a concept in a graphical user interface
a visual representation (of an object or scene or person or abstraction) produced on a surface
x: they showed us the pictures of their wedding
a movie is a series of images projected so rapidly that the eye integrates them

s.d: a conventional religious painting in oil on a small wooden panel; venerated in the Eastern Church
An image, symbol, picture, portrait, or other representation, usually as an object of religious devotion.
A type of religious painting portraying a saint or scene from Scripture, often done on wooden panels.
x: Last week the Archdiocese sent emmissaries to investigate the icon and decided that the tears were not a hoax, Father Koufos said.

s.d: A person or thing that is the best example of a certain profession or some doing.
x: That man is an icon in the business; he personifies loyalty and good business sense.
Barbie is viewed as an icon of American culture in her new biography, Barbie: Her Life and Times (Crown, $25), written by Billy Boy, a clothing and jewelry designer in Paris.

s.d: A small picture that represents something.
x: Click the loudspeaker icon to configure audio settings.

s.d: (informal) A small picture that represents something.: An image used to represent a user; an avatar or profile picture.
x: Is it okay if I use your drawing as my icon?

s.d: A word, character, or sign whose form reflects and is determined by the referent; onomatopoeic words are necessarily all icons.

iconic.e: From Late Latin īconicus, from Ancient Greek εἰκονικός (eikonikós). By surface analysis, icon + -ic.

s.d: relating to or having the characteristics of an icon
Distinctive, characteristic, indicative of identity.
x: an iconic move in martial arts

s.d: (figuratively) Famously and distinctively representative of its type.
x: For younger musicians, Coltrane’s death became one of those iconic events that stays vividly in the mind.
She angrily turned, giving me my favorite view, that iconic view of a woman from the rear.

s.d: Representing something; symbolic.
x: an iconic gesture in sign language
A portrait of a person is to a considerable extent iconic, but is not completely so since the painted canvas does not have the texture of the skin, or the capacities for speech and motion, […]

s.d: the orientation of an iconoclast
(uncountable) The belief in, participation in, or sanction of destroying religious icons and other symbols or monuments, usually with religious or political motives.
(figuratively, uncountable) A challenge to a widely held belief, tradition or cherished institution.

iconoclast.e: Borrowed from French iconoclaste and its etymon Medieval Latin īconoclastēs, from Medieval Greek εἰκονοκλάστης (eikonoklástēs, literally “image breaker”). By surface analysis, icono- + -clast.

s.d: a destroyer of images used in religious worship
someone who attacks cherished ideas or traditional institutions
(historical) One who destroys religious images or icons, especially an opponent of the Orthodox Church in the 8th and 9th centuries, or a Puritan during the European Reformation.
x: In the days of the early Christian church, people who opposed the veneration (reverence) of images were called iconoclasts.

s.d: One who opposes orthodoxy and religion; one who adheres to the doctrine of iconoclasm.
One who attacks cherished beliefs; a maverick.
x: Relishing the role of iconoclast, he confounded the scientific establishment by dismissing the consensus about the perils of man-made climate change as “tribal group-thinking.”

s.d: the branch of art history that studies visual images and their symbolic meaning (especially in social or political terms)

icosahedron.e: From Ancient Greek εἰκοσάεδρον (eikosáedron), from εἴκοσι (eíkosi, “twenty”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “face of a geometrical solid”). Equivalent to icosa- + -hedron.

s.d: any polyhedron having twenty plane faces
A regular icosahedron: one of the Platonic solids, all of whose faces are regular (equilateral) triangles

ictal.e: From ictus + -al, from Latin ictus (“a blow”).

s.d: of or relating to a seizure or convulsion

s.d: A medicine for jaundice.

s.d: (US, slang) To be wearing an excessive amount of jewelry, especially of the high-quality and expensive kind.
x: Your bitch's a regular bitch, you're calling her wifey, I fucked her, I feed her fast food, you're keeping her icy.
